statement: Greek Catholics who lived in Senné were baptised, married and buried in the Iňačovce (Solymos) parish, so they are in the Iňačovce Greek Catholic register and not in the Senné book.
basis: The 1734 visitation counted about 40 adults of the Greek rite inside the Senné Roman Catholic parish and found a separate Greek Catholic parish at Iňačovce, under 4 km away. Senné never had a Greek Catholic church or school.
test: The Solymos entry in the 1782-1787 parish reorganisation papers (PL-R-031), or any Mukachevo eparchy directory: do they list Szenna as a daughter village? Failing that, a residence of Szenna in the Iňačovce register.
resolution: A record in hand shows it. The Demko agent holds an entry of 10 December 1861 from the Iňačovce Greek Catholic book whose residence column reads Szenna (DM-D-037 @538d6b5), beside entries for Jesztreb and Solymos in the same book. The parish chronicle, a register index and the eparchy's present listing all agree. The strip's page header is not visible; the book is identified by the officiant's title on a sister entry of 1889.

log.note: The Iňačovce chronicle counts 245 Greek Catholics in Senné within its parish district; a register index gives the district of the 1811-1898 book as Iňačovce, Jastrabie, Senné and Stretava; the eparchy lists Senné as a filial today. Not yet seen: a Mukachevo directory, or an entry in the book itself with a Senné residence. That is what would solve it.
The named test was a Senné residence in the Iňačovce register. DM-D-037 is that.

The archive's catalogue, read by this agent, gives the parish district of the Iňačovce Greek Catholic register as Iňačovce, Jastrabie, Senné and Stretava. The Duska agent's 58 strips from the book show the same residences.

statement: Senné and Iňačovce stayed inside Slovakia from 1938 to 1945. Neither was annexed by Hungary, and no Hungarian-administration records exist for them for those years.
basis: Raised because the border moved twice within a few kilometres of both villages, and the neighbouring Sobrance district was annexed whole.
test: An official list of municipalities of the wartime Slovak Republic.
resolution: Both villages are in the 1940 figures of the Slovak state's Lexikón obcí under the Michalovce district: Senné with 171 houses, Iňačovce with 190. The Senné municipal history adds that after March 1939 the Hungarian border lay about 2 km from the village, with Blatná Polianka, Bežovce and Vysoká nad Uhom on the far side. The border protocol of 4 April 1939 confirms it from the other side: the line ran along the boundary between Senné and Bežovce and between Iňačovce and Blatná Polianka, with both family villages on the Slovak side.

log.note: Protocol text added as a second, independent source.

statement: The 'K. Sz.' in the 1838 gift note of the Duska agent's Folder 1 is Kis-Szeretva, today Stretavka, and the donor's village lay inside the Senné parish.
basis: The Duska agent read the place as 'K. Sz[eretva?]'. The 1734 visitation lists Stretavka among the filials of Senné, a few kilometres to the south-west. A local noblewoman giving a veil to her own parish church is the ordinary case.
test: A Szatmár diocese directory for the 1830s listing the filials of Szenna. Separately, whether a Kulin family held land at Kisszeretva.

log.note: Two Kulin landlords are in the urbarial table for Kisszeretva, Fényes names Kulin among its landlords in 1851, and the family proved its nobility in Ung in 1807. Kisszeretva was a filial of Szenna about 1799 and in 1917. The abbreviation itself is still only read, not proved: the test is a Szatmár directory of the 1830s or a clearer image of the note.

statement: Under Hungary the two villages sat in different districts of Ung county: Szenna under Nagykapos, Solymos under Szobránc. District-level papers for the two families would then be in two different series.
basis: First recalled from training. Now sourced: Hungarian reference pages place Ungszenna in the Nagykapos district and Solymos in the Szobránc district, and a study of the 1904 renaming lists Ungszenna among the Nagykapos district names.
test: The entries for Szenna and Solymos in the 1913 gazetteer of Hungary or the 1910 census volume.

log.note: Three secondary sources agree for Szenna; one, seen as an extract, for Solymos. The 1913 gazetteer itself has still not been opened.

statement: The Mukachevo eparchy series for the Ung district, 1826-1938, held at Uzhhorod, includes entries for Solymos (Iňačovce). This is a statement about a record set. It is not this agent's odds on why any one record is in Uzhhorod; for that see PL-H-015 and PL-H-016.
basis: Iňačovce belonged to the Mukachevo eparchy, whose bishop sat at Uzhhorod. The series begins in 1826, the year before the law of 1827 that ordered second copies of church registers to be lodged with the county, and its catalogue description says it covers many places of the eparchy in Ungvár and the Ung district. The Prešov catalogue lists second-copy volumes for Zemplén parishes but none for the Ung parishes read so far, so Ung's second copies are somewhere else.
test: The locality list inside FamilySearch catalogue 1411329, or the fond inventory at the Zakarpattia archive: is Solymos there, and for which years?

log.note: Tagged X-Q-01. New and relevant: the Iňačovce church archive was damaged by lightning in 1929 and fire in 1930, which is one more reason a later baptism might survive only as a copy held elsewhere.

The second research pass could not open FamilySearch catalogue 1411329 either. Still open. New in X-Q-01: no Greek Catholic volume for Iňačovce later than 1898 is in the Prešov state archive (PL-R-003).

New for X-Q-01: a note dated 1934 in the Iňačovce volume for 1870-1898 shows that volume outlived the fire of 1930. That removes one reason to think the parish's books were lost, but says nothing about the volumes begun in 1899.

log.effect: 55 to 60; reworded; no longer filed under X-Q-01
log.note: The coordinator asked whether this entry is a possibility or an explanation. It is a statement about what a series contains. The 1827 law is now sourced and no longer recalled. The locality list has still not been opened.

statement: The 1869 household sheets for Szenna and Solymos survive in the Ung county collection at Berehove.
basis: A researcher reports that the Ung county questionnaires are held there. No village list was given, and survival is usually patchy.
test: The collection's inventory, or a written query to the Zakarpattia state archive naming both villages.

log.note: A survey of archive holdings reports sheets for 214 Ung settlements at Berehove, fond 7/2, marked as to be checked. Another source says the Ung records have not been filmed. Szenna is not named in either.
Not researched in the second pass.

statement: A household list of about 1754 that counts beehives is a county tax conscription, not an urbarium, and belongs to the Ung county archive now in Ukraine.
basis: The owner told the Duska agent of a c. 1754 urbarial record with two beehives (its prior PR-3). The urbarial survey proper dates from the reign's later years and its published tables count plots and tenants, not hives. Tax conscriptions of the 1750s did count hives. From training and unchecked.
test: The heading and archive reference on the image itself, when the Duska agent receives it.

log.note: The research pass found no Ung county conscription for 1750-1760 and no fond number. Still open.

question: X-Q-02
statement: The 'Viszoka' of the 1882 baptism strip is not Vysoká nad Uhom.
basis: Raised as promised to the coordinator. The owner's file label says Čičarovce, which is a different village; that label is a prior, not evidence (X-004). Vysoká nad Uhom has its own Greek Catholic parish church today. The entry gives house number 132, so the village had at least that many houses in 1882.
test: The number of houses in Viszoka in the 1880 census or the 1877 gazetteer; which parish served its Greek Catholics and its Roman Catholics in 1882; the page header of the strip.
resolution: Viszoka had 142 houses in 1880, so house 132 fits. Ung county had one Viszoka. Its Greek Catholic parish was Čičarovce, whose priest from 1882 was Ján Csurgovics, the name read on the strips. And the Demko agent holds a 1906 record giving the same man's birthplace as Magasrév, the later Hungarian name of this village. The Viszoka of 1882 is Vysoká nad Uhom.

log.note: To be tested in the next research pass, on Vysoká nad Uhom and Čičarovce.
House count, parish and priest all fit Vysoká nad Uhom. Retired, as the Demko agent suggested.

question: X-Q-02
statement: The 1882 baptism strip is cut from the Greek Catholic register of Čičarovce (Csicser): Prešov state archive, church registers catalogue no. 182, births 1857-1886.
basis: Vysoká nad Uhom was a Greek Catholic filial of Čičarovce from 1806 to the 1940s. The parish priest from 1882 to 1886 was Ján Csurgovics. The Prešov catalogue lists Vysoká in the district of that parish and gives volume no. 182 for the years. Strips of 1875, 1879 and 1883 in the Demko repo are signed by the Csicser Greek Catholic pastors of those years. The Roman Catholics of Viszoka belonged to Pavlovce, never to Čičarovce.
test: The page header or volume label of the strip, or the entry found at no. 36 of 1882 in volume no. 182.

log.note: This is the Places ruling on X-Q-02: a Greek Catholic register, and specifically that of Čičarovce. The owner's folder label named the right parish. It stays short of solved until the header or the entry in the volume is seen.
The catalogue, read by this agent, confirms that Vysoká nad Uhom is in the Roman Catholic district of Pavlovce nad Uhom, not of Čičarovce.

statement: The baptism copies of 1894 and 1895 naming Gönyű and Szina are from the Greek Catholic register of Belža, whose original for those years is in the Košice state archive.
basis: Gönyű and Szina were filials of the Greek Catholic mother church of Bölzse in 1774-1782, 1792 and 1806 and are under Belža today. The Belža register is catalogued for 1791-1896. No source puts either village under another Greek Catholic parish.
test: The entries themselves in the Belža volume for 1894 and 1895, or a directory of the Prešov eparchy for the 1890s.

log.note: Answers the Duska agent's first question. The owner's folder label named the right parish here too. The key source was seen only as an extract.

statement: The unidentified '-falva' village of the Belža copies is Bernátfalva, Búzafalva or Csontosfalva, the three villages now inside Valaliky.
basis: Valaliky is the only present filial of the Belža parish that contains villages with Hungarian names in -falva. All three were small and close by.
test: The surviving letters of the name on the copy, against the three; a Prešov eparchy directory of the 1890s listing Bölzse's filials.

log.note: Nothing shows that any of the three was under Bölzse and not under Kassa town in 1894.

statement: Vysoká nad Uhom was inside Slovakia from April 1939 to 1944: taken by Hungarian troops in the fighting of March 1939, but not ceded.
basis: The border protocol of 4 April 1939 runs the line along its boundaries with Lekárovce and Bežovce. The Slovak state's list for 1940 has Vysoká in the Michalovce district with 230 houses, while Bežovce, Blatná Polianka, Blatné Remety, Lekárovce and Čičarovce are absent from it. Against: two municipal histories speak of Hungarian occupation, and a census database labels the village Hungarian in 1941; the 1940 list also shows its population as 0.
test: The Hungarian gazetteer of 1941 or 1944: is Magasrév in it? Or the printed Lexikón obcí of 1942 for the population figure.

log.note: Raised because this agent has now said both things about this village. The 1940 list was re-read for it on 12 Nov.

statement: The two baptism strips of about 1887 with residences at Sztrajnyán and Lasztomér come from the Michalovce and Lastomír registers: Sztrajnyán from a Michalovce book (Greek Catholic no. 673 or Roman Catholic no. 667), Lasztomér from the Lastomír Greek Catholic book (no. 531).
basis: The archive's catalogue puts Stráňany in both Michalovce parish districts and gives Lastomír a Greek Catholic register of its own from 1860. The Demko agent reads the two strips as being from two different books, and the Sztrajnyán entry as one made by mistake that belongs in another book.
test: The rite of the parents on each strip; the page header; or the entries found in the volumes named.

log.note: Answers the Demko agent's question DM→PL-003. 'Sztrajnyán' is itself a doubtful reading, and Šamudovce is a second candidate for Lastomír.

statement: The Senné copy-book pages of 1837 to 1840 in the Duska agent's Folder 1 are the bishop's notes written from the back of the Senné Roman Catholic marriage volume for 1863-1886: Prešov state archive, church registers catalogue no. 1090, microfilm 287.
basis: The archive's catalogue describes volume no. 1090 as holding, from its reverse side, notes by the bishop of Szatmár for 1837-1840. The Duska agent's ten pages are dated entries of 1837 to 1840, countersigned as revised, and one cites a district meeting at Nagykapos, the district Senné lay in. Štefan Rácz was parish priest of Senné in those years.
test: On FamilySearch film 1793682, the item that holds Senné marriages 1863-1886: the copy-book pages should be at its end, upside down or reversed. Or the owner's film and image numbers (RQ-4).

log.note: Found while answering the Duska agent's question about volume no. 1089. It names the volume and film for DUS:H-010 and RQ-4. Held under solved because this agent has the catalogue's description, not the pages.

question: X-Q-01
statement: For a birth of 1906 at Solymos, the record in Uzhhorod is the county's second copy of the state civil register made at Alsókánya.
basis: State registration began on 1 October 1895 and its books were kept in two copies; county archives hold the second copies as a series. The county seat of Ung was Ungvár. A civil entry of August 1906 for Solymos is in hand, headed at Alsókánya. So a second copy of that very entry was owed to Uzhhorod. Not shown for Ung by any source read here: that the second copies went to the county and survive in the Zakarpattia archive. That step rests on the practice in other counties.
test: The fond and series title of the Uzhhorod record (RQ-6). A second copy of a civil register will be a printed Hungarian state form with a registrar's signature, not a priest's.

log.note: This agent's odds on the explanation, as the coordinator asked. Place evidence cannot separate this from PL-H-016: both kinds of copy would have been sent to the same town.

question: X-Q-01
statement: The record in Uzhhorod is a Greek Catholic entry held by the eparchy: a second copy or the bishop's own series.
basis: The eparchy's series at Uzhhorod runs to 1938 (PL-R-004), and no Iňačovce Greek Catholic volume after 1898 is in the Prešov archive, so a baptism of 1906 has no other known home. Against: whether Solymos is in that series is not checked, and the second-copy volumes seen in the Prešov catalogue stop in 1895, when state registration began.
test: As PL-H-015. A church copy will name the officiating priest and the godparents.

log.note: The rival to PL-H-015 on this board. The two sum to 85; the rest is for a record of some other kind or a birthplace now in Ukraine.

statement: The 45 Reformed strips in the Duska agent's Folder F-007 are from the register kept for the Iňačovce filial of the Lúčky Reformed parish: Prešov state archive, church registers catalogue no. 592/1, microfilm 88-89.
basis: The archive's catalogue lists a register kept for the Iňačovce filial alone, with births from 1819 to 1927. The strips run from 1825 to 1921 and every residence but one is Solymos, which is what a book for one filial would show and what the mother church's own book would not. No other Reformed register covers Iňačovce.
test: A page header or volume label; or one of the entries found in no. 592/1.

log.note: The Duska agent asked this agent to rule on which book (DUS:H-043, at 70). The match is on years, residence and denomination. Short of solved: no header and no archive image in hand.
